list.listitem: The diagnosis of upper respiratory tract infection (RTI) is based on clinical signs and symptoms. This is an acute infection that is typically viral in origin and in which sinus, pharyngeal, and lower airway symptoms are present, but not prominent. B

Antibiotics are ineffective for the treatment of the common cold in children and adults. No antibiotics and delayed antibiotics strategies reduce the use of antibiotics compared to the strategy of immediate antibiotics. A

Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic treatment of immunocompetent adults and children with acute RTIs decreases mortality, antibiotic use, and antibiotic-related adverse events. Similarly, C-reactive protein (CRP) point-of-care tests decrease antibiotic prescription in the primary care setting. A
Oral antihistamines early in symptom course and multiple doses of intranasal decongestants may provide symptom relief in adults. B
The mean duration of illness is 7 to 14 days; most patients feel better within the first week. However, cough may persist for up to 3 weeks. B

background.definition: Nonspecific upper respiratory infection (URI) is typically viral in origin and presents with symptoms that are referred to as the common cold. Clinical features include headache, sneezing, sore throat, rhinorrhea, malaise, and cough.

list.listitem: Children: 6 to 8 common colds per year.
Adults: 2 to 4 common colds per year.
The annual cost for antibiotic prescriptions for URIs is $227 million.
The common cold causes approximately 20 million lost work days and 21 million lost school days.
There are 25 million ambulatory care visits annually for URIs.
Rhinoviruses are the most common cause. Other viral causes include coronavirus, influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, adenovirus, and enterovirus.
Various respiratory viruses have different mechanisms that lead to common cold symptoms.
Our understanding of the pathophysiology of the common cold comes from studying the rhinovirus.
The virus infects nasal mucosa or eyes through direct contact or aerosolized particles.
Infection of the nasal mucosa leads to vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, which leads to nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea.
Stimulation of the mucous glands also leads to rhinorrhea.
Inflammatory mediators contribute to malaise, headache, and myalgia.
Based on very low-certainty evidence from 1 RCT, the adenovirus vaccine does not appear to be more effective than placebo in preventing the common cold.
Daily high-dose vitamin D (2000 IU), compared to daily standard-dose vitamin D (400 IU), does not reduce wintertime viral upper RTIs in healthy children 1 to 5 years of age.

In a meta-analysis of 6 case-control studies, physical measures that were effective in preventing the spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) were handwashing more than 10 times daily (OR = 0.45; 95% CI, 0.36-0.57; NNT = 4), wearing masks (OR = 0.32; 95% CI, 0.25-0.40; NNT = 6), wearing N95 masks (OR = 0.09; 95% CI, 0.03-0.30; NNT = 3), wearing gloves (OR = 0.43; 95% CI, 0.29-0.65; NNT = 5), wearing gowns (OR = 0.23; 95% CI, 0.14-0.37; NNT = 5), and handwashing, masks, gloves, and gowns combined (OR = 0.09; 95% CI, 0.02-0.35; NNT = 3).

Based on limited evidence, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (eg, walking, treadmill, biking, or combination) does not appear to affect acute RTI occurrence (low-certainty evidence), but appears to decrease its severity (moderate-certainty evidence).

Among children under 5 years of age with undifferentiated acute respiratory infections, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence that prescribing antibiotics (eg, amoxicillin/clavulanate, ampicillin) prevents secondary bacterial infections like otitis media or pneumonia.

The diagnosis of upper RTI (common cold) is used when there is an acute infection that is typically viral in origin and in which sinus, pharyngeal, and lower airway symptoms are present, but not prominent. B
Purulent nasal discharge or sputum does not predict bacterial infection or benefit from antibiotics. A
Respiratory viral testing should not be ordered for healthy, immunocompetent children presenting with typical viral RTI symptoms; diagnosis should be made clinically. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Wide range of presentation but can mimic acute upper RTI; a Cochrane review noted individual symptoms of COVID-19 have poor diagnositic accuracy but anosmia or ageusia may be a helpful red flag feature, and that presence of cough in the correct clinical context may warrant further testing
Upper RTI symptoms that have not improved after 10 days or worsen after 5 days
Fever, tonsillopharyngeal erythema and exudates, anterior cervical adenopathy, absence of cough
Abrupt onset of constitutional and respiratory symptoms, particularly accompanied by myalgias and fatigue
Bulging, limited mobility, and erythema of tympanic membrane; air-fluid level or bubbles of air may be visible; otorrhea; distinct otalgia
Fever, tachypnea, tachycardia, abnormal chest examination, or abnormal chest x-ray

list.listitem: The diagnosis of upper RTI is based on clinical signs and symptoms. This is an acute infection that is typically viral in origin and in which sinus, pharyngeal, and lower airway symptoms are present, but not prominent.
Purulent nasal discharge or sputum occurs when inflammatory cells or sloughed mucosal epithelial cells are present.
Eighty percent to 90% of patients with the common cold develop purulent rhinitis.
Diagnostic tests are not indicated.

In a randomized trial of acutely ill children presenting to the pediatric ED (n=1243), point-of-care testing for respiratory pathogens did not reduce antibiotic prescriptions or affect imaging use, hospital admissions, or ED returns.
Patients with signs and symptoms suggestive of a more severe infection (e.g., tachypnea, purulent sputum, or hemoptysis) should have a chest radiograph or other testing as clinically indicated.
CBC with differential is not a reliable way to distinguish viral from bacterial URI.
See algorithm in for evaluation of patients who are otherwise healthy.
Patients with risk factors for increased severity of disease (infants, the elderly, smokers, those with chronic disease, and those who are immunocompromised) should consult a health care provider.
Do not use antibiotics to treat the common cold in children and adults. Not only is it ineffective, it causes significant adverse events. A

Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic treatment of immunocompetent adult and pediatric patients with acute respiratory infections decreases mortality, antibiotic use, and antibiotic-related adverse events. Similarly, C-reactive protein (CRP) point-of-care tests decrease antibiotic prescription in the primary care setting. A
Multiple doses of nasal decongestant may be effective for the short-term relief of congestion in adults. Evidence is insufficient to assess the effectiveness of a single dose. B
Antihistamines may reduce overall severity of symptoms in adults during the first two days of use. There is no evidence of effectiveness of antihistamines in children. B
Dextromethorphan may be effective for cough in adults with upper RTI. B

Adults and children with the common cold who received antibiotics did no better with respect to cure or persistence of symptoms than those given placebo. Moreoever, adults developed significant adverse events from antibiotics compared to placebo. Delayed antibiotics strategy (provided at the time of visit, or available on return without an appointment, and time-limited), compared to immediate antibiotics strategy, reduces antibiotic use (30.6% vs 93.4%, p = 0.001; moderate-certainty evidence) with little, if any, impact on satisfaction and no increase in harms. No antibiotics strategy for acute RTI has similar outcomes (ie, symptom control and disease complications) compared to delayed antibiotics approach, while likely resulting to the least use of antibiotics among the three strategies and similar patient satisfaction as delayed antibiotics strategy.
For adult patients with upper RTI presenting predominantly as acute laryngitis (<3 weeks), oral antibiotics do not appear to be effective in improving objective outcomes.

A Cochrane review of individual patient data from 26 RCTs involving 6,708 immunocompetent adult and pediatric patients from 12 countries found that, compared to usual care, procalcitonin-guided initiation or discontinuation of antibiotics for acute respiratory infections (in ambulatory clinics, ED, hospital wards, and ICU) decreases mortality (adjusted OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.99, P=0.037), shortens antibiotic use by 2.4 days (5.7 versus 8.1 days, 95% CI ‐2.71 to ‐2.15, P<0.001), and lowers antibiotic-related adverse events (16.3% versus 22.1%, adjusted OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.82, P<0.001). The procalcitonin cutoff for the individual studies ranged from 0.25 μg/L to 1.0 μg/L. All the trials used high-sensitivity procalcitonin assays, hence no point-of-care tests were evaluated. The review (published in 2017) estimated the cost of procalcitonin test between US $20 to US $30. Given the possible cost savings from decreased use of antibiotics and other health resources, the authors recommend that future studies should evaluate the cost-effectiveness of procalcitonin.

Similarly, a Cochrane review of 12 RCTs involving 10,218 immunocompetent adults and children found that C-reactive protein (CRP) point-of-care tests for acute respiratory infections in primary care decrease antibiotic prescriptions (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.86; I² = 79%; moderate‐certainty evidence). However, illness recovery rates and mortality were similar between CRP testing and control groups. Cutoff values for CRP ranged between 40 mg/L and 100 mg/L.

A Belgian cluster randomized trial involving 171 primary care practices found that a simple algorithm plus selective use of CRP can safely reduce antibiotic use in acutely ill children compared to usual care. The cutoff for CRP was 5 mg/L, which triggered a recommendation of antibiotics or additional testing (e.g., urinalysis, x-ray). Full recovery was similar for the intervention and control groups (4.6 vs 4.7 days). Antibiotic prescribing at the index consultation was low in both groups (compared to the U.S.), was lower in the intervention group (16% vs 22%; adjusted absolute risk reduction [aARR] 5.1%; 95% CI 1.0-8.5%; NNT = 20), and was also lower 30 days after the index visit (aARR 2.4%; 0.2-4.2%; NNT = 42). Finally, safety outcomes were comparable between groups.
Antihistamines may reduce overall severity of symptoms in adults during the first two days of use. There is no evidence of effectiveness of antihistamines in children.
Dextromethorphan may be effective for cough in adults with upper RTI.
Acetaminophen may help relieve rhinorrhea and nasal obstruction but does not appear to help with other cold symptoms.

Naproxen may have beneficial effects on the symptoms of headache, malaise, myalgia, and cough, based on an RCT involving patients with rhinovirus RTI. A Cochrane review of 9 NSAIDs trials demonstrated significant benefit for headache, ear pain, and muscle and joint pain (related to the analgesic effects of NSAIDs); there was borderline benefit on malaise, and no benefit on cough or rhinorrhea.

For the treatment of fever in children, a Cochrane review of 6 RCTs involving 915 patients concluded that both simultaneous and alternating (every 1 to 4 hours) use of acetaminophen and ibuprofen results in better fever control than monotherapy using either medication (low- to moderate-quality evidence).

Acetylcysteine and carbocysteine are mucolytics widely used in Europe, Brazil, and Africa for bronchitic cough. A Cochrane review found limited evidence for its use in children age 2 years and older with acute upper and lower RTIs, and cautioned against its routine use for younger patients.

Antihistamine-analgesic-decongestant combinations may have some general symptomatic benefit in adults and older children. There is no evidence of effectiveness in young children. Overall, the Cochrane review found paucity of strong data on the efficacy of this combo, warned against the risks of adverse events, and highlighted the FDA warning on nasal formulations containing phenylpropanolamine. B

Single-dose nasal decongestants have unclear benefits for the common cold. Multiple doses of nasal decongestants may have small, short-term benefits for nasal congestion in adults. The safety and efficacy of topical nasal decongestants in children is uncertain.
Intranasal corticosteroids do not seem to provide symptomatic relief, but evidence is limited and of poor quality.

Based on a systematic review of 7 RCTs enrolling 2,144 patients with the common cold, intranasal ipratropium bromide appears effective in decreasing rhinorrhea but not nasal congestion. Additionally, ipratropium bromide caused more adverse events which were mostly mild and transient.
An inhaled anticholinergic ipratropium bromide may be effective for cough suppression in adults.

Probiotics may be more beneficial than placebo or no treatment in preventing acute upper RTI in adults and children, as well as in reducing duration of acute upper RTI episodes and decreasing antibiotic use. A small RCT (n = 128) conducted in the emergency department among children presenting with fever and acute upper RTI found that probiotics reduces fever duration by 2 days compared with placebo. These findings may not apply to children with less severe symptoms.

Vitamin C prophylaxis may decrease the duration and severity of the symptoms, but supplementation did not reduce the incidence of the common cold with the exception of those participating in severe exercise or exposed to cold environments.

Four systematic reviews found that zinc administered within 24 hours of the onset of cold symptoms reduces the duration and severity in healthy adults, but may result to higher rates of non-serious adverse events. Zinc supplementation does not appear to prevent colds in a clinically meaningful way.

A systematic review of 25 RCTs concluded that supplementation with vitamin D was safe and protected against acute RTI in children and adults. In contrast, a Cochrane review only found 1 large RCT which did not find vitamin D beneficial in preventing respiratory infection in children under five years of age.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to support use of garlic in preventing or treating the common cold; one trial supported its role in prevention.

Preparations based on aerial parts from Echinacea purpurea may be effective for early treatment but research results are not consistent. Other echinacea preparations have not been proven to be of benefit.
In a meta-analysis, ginseng (when taken for 8-16 weeks) significantly shortened the duration of colds by 6.2 days (2 trials; 95% CI, 3.4-9.0).

A Cochrane review found no evidence to support the efficacy of homeopathic medicinal products for improving cure rates or preventing recurrences of acute RTI in children (low- to very low-certainty evidence).

There is insufficient evidence for the efficacy of oral Astragalus (Huang qi), a traditional Chinese medicine, for preventing frequent episodes of acute RTIs in children. Similarly, other Chinese medicinal herbs have uncertain efficacy for the common cold. Rigorous trials are needed.

Umckaloabo, a South African herbal remedy derived from the roots of Pelargonium sidoides, may have beneficial effects in adults with the common cold, but its overal efficacy is uncertain due to the very low quality of evidence.
Both no antibiotics strategy and delayed antibiotics approach reduce use of antibiotics and do not decrease patient satisfaction.
Patient and public education interventions are effective in reducing antibiotic prescribing.

Clinician empathy (defined as perfect score on an empathy scale), as perceived by patients with a common cold, may decrease cold duration (by about 1 day) and severity. It also appears to increase cytokine interleukin-8.
A Cochrane review found no RCTs to evaluate the efficacy of advising patients with acute RTI to increase fluid intake.

There is no clear evidence of benefits or harms with the use of heated, humidified air for patients with the common cold or acute upper RTIs, based on 6 trials with 387 participants. In a randomized trial of 889 patients at least 3 years of age, advice to use steam inhalation with or without regular or as-needed analgesic dosing did not improve symptoms.
Small trials indicate saline nasal irrigation may relieve the symptoms of acute upper RTI.
Infection of the upper respiratory tract may lead to eustachian tube dysfunction, which plays a role in acute otitis media.
Infection may trigger asthma exacerbations in children and adults.
Infection may trigger chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbations.
Approximately 8% of cases of the common cold are complicated by acute bacterial sinusitis in young children.
The mean duration of the common cold is 7 to 14 days; most patients feel better within the first week. C
Cough may persist up to 3 weeks. C
Self-limited disease.
The mean duration of the common cold is 7 to 14 days; most patients feel better within the first week.
Cough may persist up to 3 weeks in adults and children; consider pertussis for persistent cough.
The prognosis and natural history are the same.
None recommended.
Advise the patient to contact a health care provider if symptoms do not improve after 10 days or worsen after 5 days.
Educate patients about the differences between viral and bacterial infections.

Discuss good hygiene (e.g., patients should cover their mouth and nose while coughing and wash hands to prevent transmission). Recommend coughing inside the elbow, which will avoid hand contamination.
Discuss the dangers of antibiotic use, including adverse events and bacterial resistance.

In a randomized controlled trial of 1072 adults with a mean age of 76 years, the group taking a fermented probiotic (Lactobacillus casei) for 3 months had upper respiratory infections that were 3 days shorter in duration than the group taking placebo, with no difference in the overall number of URIs or adverse events. The mechanism of action is unclear.

Pregnancy risk categories for commonly used medications: Acetaminophen—B Dextromethorphan—C Chlorpheniramine—B Ipratropium—B Guaifenesin—C Naproxen—B in first and second trimester. D in third trimester. Should be used sparingly because of possibility of adverse effects on fetus Oxymetazoline—C Pseudoephedrine—B
Antitussives and antihistamines are not effective for symptomatic relief.
Antihistamine-analgesic-decongestant combinations have some general benefit older children. There is no evidence of effectiveness in young children.

In children between the ages of 2 and 11 years with upper RTI symptoms for at least 7 days, application of vapor rub improved symptom scores and children and parents’ ability to sleep compared to petrolatum or placebo.
A single dose of honey can reduce cough severity and sleep disturbance in children; it should not be given to infants because of the risk of botulism.
Nasal decongestants are generally not recommended since their safety and efficacy are uncertain.
Acetaminophen is effective for fever reduction.
Nasal suctioning in infants may relieve congestion.

algorithm.title: Evaluation of the Patient With Acute Respiratory Infection.

cell.label: Patient reports symptoms of: headache, sneezing, sore throat, rhinorrhea, malaise, or cough
Symptoms of acute rhinosinusitis: URI symptoms that have not improved after 10 days or worsen after 5-7 days.
Symptoms of streptococcal pharyngitis: fever, tonsillopharyngeal erythema and exudates, anterior cervical adenopathy, absence of cough.
Symptoms of influenza: abrupt onset of constitutional and respiratory symptoms, particularly accompanied by myalgias and fatigue.
Symptoms of otitis media: bulging, limited mobility, erythema, or air fluid level of tympanic membrane; otorrhea; or distinct otalgia.
Symptoms of pneumonia: fever, tachypnea, tachycardia, abnormal chest examination, or abnormal chest x-ray.
Symptoms of common cold: sinus, pharyngeal, and lower airway symptoms are present, but not prominent.
